newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Greenspan unleashes European stocks, dollar.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Greenspan unleashes European stocks, dollar.

text.p: European stock markets shot to record highs on Wednesday, unleashed by U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan -- the man who only last month wiped billions off share values by warning of "irrational exuberance".
The dollar also took heart from Greenspan's upbeat report on the U.S. economy, surging to levels against the yen and mark not seen for more than three years.
For the markets, what Greenspan did not say in his testimony to the U.S. Senate on Tuesday was as important as what he did say. December's warning to investors was conspicuously absent.
"Greenspan's speech seems to have been taken very well and he didn't take the chance to knock Wall Street down to earth," said one London dealer.
Only 24 hours earlier, investors feared that Greenspan would repeat his warning that world markets were overheating, which sent stock markets reeling across the globe last month.

Since then investors have regained their courage and the Dow Jones Industrial average has risen about 400 points. But this time Greenspan, the epitome of the prudent central banker, described the stock markets' performance only as breathtaking.
That was all the markets needed. The Dow closed up 40.03 points at a record 6,883.90 on Tuesday and European markets followed suit on Wednesday.

At 0955 GMT, leading European markets were in record territory. London's FTSE 100 index gained 31.4 points to 4,226.9, in Frankfurt the DAX was up 62.14 at 3,038.85 and the Paris CAC-40 surged 33.47 to 2,443.35.

"The main point is that he seemed by no means as concerned about inflation as many people thought he would be," said the head of sales at a major British investment bank. "Greenspan's speech suggests the chances of a near-term U.S. rate rise have receded, although you can't say they've entirely disappeared."

The dollar stormed through 1.64 marks and flirted with 119 yen, fuelled largely by Greenspan's positive report, including his comment that tight U.S. labour markets had not stoked inflation. At midmorning it was at 1.6415 marks and 118.96.
Outside the U.S., Italian interest rate cuts and a weak German business climate survey on Tuesday buoyed the dollar as they pointed to lower rates in Europe, analysts said.

Concern over the health of Russian President Boris Yeltsin was yet another spur upwards for dollar/mark, while indications that Japanese interest rates would stay low enthused dollar/yen. "It's all coming together. People have set in their minds clear targets of the mid-1.60s against the mark...and 120 to 125 against the yen," said Stephen Hannah, director of research at IBJ International in London.
The dollar surged to 118.96 yen and 1.6415 marks from Tuesday's late European levels of 117.78 and 1.6240.
The FTSE 100 index of leading British shares was up 31.4 points at 4,226.9.
In Paris, the CAC-40 share index was 33.47 higher at 2,443.35. The 30-share DAX index in Frankfurt was up 62.14 at 3,038.85.
Gold fell to $350.55 from a $353.65 close in London on Tuesday. Silver was at $4.71 after closing Tuesday at $4.73.
